I agree to participate in a study that is investigating body awareness.  I understand that my participation is entirely voluntary: I can leave the study at any time and this will have no bearing on the credit I receive, nor will it have any other undesirable consequences. The following points have been explained to me:

 
Purpose: The purpose of this research is to use functional neuroimaging (fMRI) to explore how the brain represents sensation from within our own bodies.  I understand that I will be asked to carry out tasks tapping various mental skills.  The benefits I may expect to receive from this study are: (a) an appreciation of research on person body awareness, (b) an opportunity to contribute to scientific research, and (c) financial compensation for my time ($65).
 

Procedure: The procedure, lasting 2 hours, will be as follows: In the MRI, I will monitor breath while wearing a respiration monitor; outside the MRI, I will be asked to fill out some questionnaires measuring different aspects of my mood and body awareness.
 

Brain imaging: The purpose of this research project is to better understand how brain activity can help us to understand person perception and learning. We will take scans which show the structure of your brain, and scans which measure brain activity while perform tasks we describe above. We will train you in these tasks before entering the scanner. In terms of duration: the two hour experiment involves:
 


	
	
		30 minutes doing training;
		1 hour in the scanner, including getting changed and completing safety screening questionnaires; 
		30 minutes of questionnaires. 
	
	



During the scan, you will be asked to lie as still as you can on your back in the scanner bore (a giant magnet that looks like a toilet paper roll on its side). You will be equipped with the following: 


	headphones that will muffle the scanner noise (it is very loud when it is running) and allow us to communicate with you in the scanner;
	a respiration monitor around your chest (a thin stretchy belt);
	a cardiac monitor on your hand (like a clothespin on one finger); 
	a respirator in your mouth to measure your breathing and Carbon Dioxide levels- this is the same as using a snorkel or scuba diving respirator, but you will still be breathing regular air from the room- we only measure your outbreath. The respirators are fully sanitized between use;
	 a squeeze bulb in your left hand which will stop the scanner at any time if you feel too uncomfortable to continue; and
	A button box under your right hand for responding to the experimental tasks (you will be able to see a computer screen reflected on a mirror above your eyes from a projector at the back of the room).



Before entering the scanner, you will fill out a Screening Questionnaire to determine that it is safe for you to enter. People with metal implants, such as surgical clips, prosthetic heart valves, neurostimulators, implanted pumps, cochlear implants, hearing aids, dentures or pacemakers should not have an MRI scan. If you have answered “Yes” to any items, you must discuss the specific information with the investigator and MRI technologist to determine that it is safe for you to participate. “Yes” answers do not automatically disqualify you from the study; they simply require follow-up questions to protect your safety and quality of the data. It is important for you to remain very still during the scanning session. Movement will not be dangerous to you, but it will make the data we collect difficult or impossible to analyse properly. You will not be asked to perform any tasks during the scan, just to lie still.



While all forms of diagnostic medical procedures involve some risk, the known hazards associated with MRI scanning are negligible. There are no known adverse effects of MRI scanning on the human body. Some people do become nervous while being scanned because the magnet is not spacious and it makes loud knocking sounds. You will be provided with ear plugs or ear phones to protect your ears, as well as foam pads to make you as comfortable as possible. In addition, fMRI scans can cause some people to feel knocking, tapping, or buzzing sensations in their arms or legs. This occurrence is rare, and the sensations are completely harmless. During your time in the scanner, you can contact the operator at the console at any time simply by speaking out loud over the intercom. If you feel any discomfort, say so and we will immediately either fix the problem or end the experiment and remove you from the scanner.



The MRI scan being done is designed to answer research questions, not to examine your brain medically. This MRI scan is not a substitute for one that a doctor would order, and it may not show problems that would be picked up by a medical MRI scan. However, in the unlikely event that we note an atypical finding on your MRI scan, we will contact you to help you arrange medical follow-up to interpret the significance of the findings, if any. We may also ask a radiologist, or other health professional, to look at your scan, and by signing this consent form you agree to release the scan for review. It is possible that you could be unnecessarily worried if a problem were suspected, but not actually found.



Risks: The researchers do not foresee any risks to me for participating in this study, nor do they expect that I will experience any discomfort or stress.  Occasionally however someone who has no history of claustrophobia will experience panic in the scanner. If I do experience feelings of discomfort at any point during the study, I recognise that I am free to refrain from answering any question, or withdraw from the study at any time, without penalty, and will still receive payment for my participation regardless of my completion of the study. 



All data collected will remain strictly confidential.  Only people associated with the study will see my responses.  This consent form will be stored separately.  My responses will not be associated with my name; instead, my name will be converted to a code number when the researchers store the date. Once the study is complete and you have been awarded credit, we will immediately delete any record linking your data to you. At this point, we will not be able to remove your data from the dataset, as we will not know which data belongs to you.


	Once the study is complete and all the data has been de-identified, we will share the dataset on the Open Science Framework (osf.io), which other researchers can access. We do not believe there is any chance that someone will be able to discover your identity using this data.
	The researcher will answer any other questions about the research either now or during the course of the experiment.  If I have any other questions or concerns, I can address them to the researcher or to principal investigator:  Prof. Norman Farb, norman.farb@utoronto.ca. If you have concerns about the treatment of research participants, please contact the University of Toronto Ethics Review Office by phone at 416-946-3273, or by email at ethics.review@utoronto.ca.
	Debriefing: Upon completion of my participation, I will receive a full written explanation about the rationale and predictions underlying this experiment.  I will also receive a copy of this consent form. - Id
